extracted.intended_audience: readers of early-18th-century periodical essays / literate coffee-house public interested in manners, wit, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Short, satirical periodical essays offering rules and examples about wit, conversation, flirtation, and social conduct in early 18th-century urban society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit's proper circumference / suitability for print
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit must describe its proper circumference, and not go beyond it, lest ... it may wander to places where it is not known, and be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume lively or brilliant conversation retains its effect when printed: 'how small an appearance the prettiest things said in company, make when in print.' Be cautious in transforming spoken repartee into print; some spoken wit is best kept observed, not published. (Example: the reporter sits silent at a visit, only laying up 'what excellent things pass at such conversations'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good company / good conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good company is not merely brisk talk or a knack of saying common things; true good company 'hits her height of understanding' with sly seriousness rather than merely being quick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer wit that shows understanding and aptness over mere volubility. Examples: Mistress Giddy is 'very quick' but only utters common things; Mrs. Slim, who speaks less, 'had understanding' and 'was as good company as she.' Good company includes well-timed repartee, modesty, and the ability to 'hit her height of understanding.'

rubrics_metrics.name: How to flatter a 'Platonne' (subtle flattery)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Platonne (a professed Platonist woman) is not moved by gross panegyric; 'You are not therefore to commend, but silently consent to all she does, and says.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subtlety rather than overt praise. Do not treat her like ordinary women who respond to bold flattery; instead, quietly agree and defer, treating scorn as opinion rather than humour. Avoid sensual or literal readings of metaphysical imagery; acknowledge her intellectual stance by consenting rather than lauding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as a necessary complement to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty loses its force, if not accompanied with modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a woman's attractiveness, value modesty: 'She that has a humble opinion of herself, will have everybody's applause... while the vain creature loses approbation through too great a sense of deserving it.' In contests of charm or performance, modesty can tip undecided preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning condemned
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning is described as an 'enormity' revived in the town and worthy of censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author intends to collect and expose offences of punning as socially offensive — treat punning as a vulgar or shameful abuse of language to be discouraged in polite company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor when praising a lady
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lady's charms are spoken of 'there's no carrying a metaphor too far.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbolic metaphor is acceptable, even encouraged, in praising female beauty — the text playfully permits extravagant figurative language ('a fine woman dancing, a brandished torch of beauty') when admiring charms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require evidence of a suitor's past behaviour (credentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lover should have a certificate from the last woman he served, how he was turned away, before he was received into the service of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As practical advice for women selecting suitors: demand proof or testimony of past conduct rather than relying on a man's professions. This is proposed analogously to vetting servants (we require credentials for a footman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist impulsive sexual advances to preserve virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve chastity and resist forward behaviour: 'Any unnatural part is long taking up, and as long laying aside; therefore Mr. Sturdy may assure himself, Platonica will fly for ever from a forward behaviour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to suitors and the defended: approach with restraint and proper conduct; impudence and force are condemned and will repel virtuous women. The narrative example (a woman falling to her knees, invoking virtue) models how firm resistance maintains honour and may reform the aggressor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performances judged by modesty and apparent willingness
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging performances (e.g., dancing, comportment), outward humility or diffidence increases perceived merit over ostentatious display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two dancers equally skilled — the narrator awards 'very pretty' to the one who shows modesty and diffidence rather than the more assured performer. Modest behaviour amplifies perceived merit in social contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical 'remedies' and the timing/preparation for social cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosmetic or social 'cures' (e.g., Bickerstaff's Circumspection Water) require correct timing and constitution to be effective; they are ineffective 'in the rage of the distemper' and need preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As satire of social quick-fixes, the guidance says some behavioral corrections must be prepared for and cannot be applied during moments of excess (e.g., a bride in her first month or someone newly exalted cannot immediately benefit). Also implies skepticism of miraculous, public cures: avoid mountebank methods and prefer discreet, measured remedies.
